newsitem.title: USA: CBOT soybeans tumble on stocks ideas, weather.
newsitem.headline: CBOT soybeans tumble on stocks ideas, weather.

text.p: CBOT soybean futures ended lower Tuesday, hit by ideas USDA would not raise its 1996-97 ending stocks figures in Friday's supply and demand report, traders said.

"There seemed to be a little bit of growing disenchantment that the USDA was going to make a significant change on the supply/demand report coming out Friday," said Dale Durchholz, analyst with Agrivisor Services, a division of the Illinois Farm Bureau.
USDA in March put ending stocks at a tight 140 million bushels. The April report is due Friday.
Soybeans had rallied last week on ideas the stocks number would fall even further. USDA's 22 million bushel downward revision in the March 1 quarterly stocks supported that idea.
Meanwhile, the fundamental outlook was bleak. Taiwan overnight bought 54,000 tonnes South American soybeans and South Korea bought 85,000 tonnes Brazilian soymeal.
Weather was also deemed bearish. Forecasts called for cold, wet weather in the U.S. Midwest next week which could delay corn plantings and force farmers to plant soybeans.
Soybeans settled down 13-1/2 to two cents, with May down 13-1/2 at $8.49-1/4 per bushel.
"The weather problems we're having in parts of the Midwest are tilting people to the idea that bean acres will probably grow even more," Durchholz said.
Reports a vessel carrying Brazilian soybeans was still headed for the U.S. Gulf compounded the bearish sentiment.
"The rumor mill is that while we aren't able to track down where that vessel is, the buyer is still expecting U.S. delivery," said Bill Biedermann, director of research for Allendale Inc.
News of the Brazilian sale to a U.S. firm sent soybeans spiralling lower last week but some floor sources had speculated the soybeans would never reach U.S. soil.
The trade shrugged off reports several analytical groups cut projections for Brazil and Argentina soybeans.
Floor sources said news of drought damage had been in the market for weeks and the production losses, while significant, were no greater than expected.

Brazilian cooperative federation Fecotrigo expected soybean losses of 790,000 tonnes in Rio Grande do Sul. The state's 1996-97 crop was expected to be less than five million tonnes, compared to an initial forecast of 5.7 million tonnes.

The independent Oil World newsletter cut its Argentine crop forecast to 12.7 million tonnes from 13.0 million forecast on March 25. It also trimmed Brazil's output to 26.9 million tonnes from 27.2 million.
Technically, the May contract failed to reach a key chart point at $8.67 per bushel which prompted aggressive fund selling, Biedermann said.
"We tried for $8.67 in the May and when it was unable to get above that level, funds came in and sold," he said.
On the day, Cargill Inc sold 2.5 million bushels May, Merrill Lynch sold 2.5 million July and Refco Inc sold two million July and one million May, traders said.
Dean Witter spread two million bushels July/May at four to 4-1/2 cents, premium July. Cargill Investor Services spread 1.5 million bushels May/July at 3-1/2 cents.

In options trade, Smith Barneybpigjt 1,000 November $6.50 puts at 22-1/2 cents and sold 1,000 July $8.25 puts at 22-1/2 cents, pit sources said. Hagerty Trading bought 400 July $7.75 puts at 7-3/4 and sold 200 July $8.50 calls at 50 cents.
Soybean volume was estimated by CBOT at 53,000 contracts, compared with Monday's actual volume of 72, 834 contracts.
